title: Sovereignty Among Nations
hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.
key_points: Sovereignty means a state has supreme authority within its borders and no superior outside them.
The international system is 'anarchic' — not chaotic, but lacking a world government above states.
States are formally equal and recognize each other's authority over their territory.
With no overarching enforcer, cooperation rests on mutual interest, agreements, and power.
content_html: Domestic politics and international politics differ in one foundational way. Within a country, the state is sovereign: it holds supreme authority over its territory and people, and it can ultimately enforce its laws. But step outside the border and that structure vanishes. There is no world government standing above states the way a state stands above its citizens. Each sovereign state recognizes no superior authority over itself, and all are treated as formally equal members of the international system.
extra_html: Scholars call this condition "anarchy" — a word that here means the absence of a ruler above states, not disorder or violence. The point is structural: because there is no global sovereign to make and enforce rules, the system works very differently from a domestic one. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes sovereignty as the supreme authority of a state, and the mutual recognition of sovereignty is what lets states deal with one another as independent equals. The consequence is that international cooperation cannot simply be commanded; it has to be built. States follow rules and keep agreements largely because doing so serves their interests, because they value their reputation, and because the distribution of power among them makes some outcomes more sustainable than others. Understanding this anarchic structure is the starting point for almost every other topic in international relations — from why treaties are needed to why international organizations have the powers, and the limits, that they do.

related.title: What Government Is For
related.hook: Every society needs a way to make and enforce collective decisions — that shared system of authority is what we call government.

related.title: Treaties & International Law
related.hook: If no world government can pass laws, how do nations bind themselves at all? Largely by agreeing to — treaties are the contracts that knit the international order together.

related.title: The UN & International Organizations
related.hook: Sovereign states that answer to no one above them still build standing clubs to cooperate. The UN is the largest — a forum, not a world government.

related.title: Globalization
related.hook: The world's economies have woven together so tightly that a decision in one country ripples through all the others — that deepening interdependence is globalization.

related.title: Theories of International Relations
related.hook: Why do states behave as they do? Three big theories give rival answers — and which lens you use changes what you see in every global event.

flashcards.prompt: What does sovereignty mean for a state in the world?
flashcards.back_html: It has supreme authority within its borders and recognizes no superior authority outside them — no world government sits above it.

flashcards.prompt: What do scholars mean by calling the international system 'anarchic'?

choices.text: There is no world government above sovereign states, not that it is chaotic
That international politics is always violent
That states have no governments of their own

flashcards.explanation_html: 'Anarchy' here is structural: it means no higher authority above states, which can still cooperate and follow rules.

flashcards.prompt: Given no overarching enforcer, what mainly holds international cooperation together?

choices.text: Mutual interest, agreements, and the balance of power
A global police force that arrests states

flashcards.explanation_html: Without a world government, states cooperate because it serves their interests, backed by agreements and the realities of power.
